abstract: Solid-state batteries (SSBs) are promising next-generation energy-storage systems because of their potential for improved safety and high energy density. However, their practical implementation remains limited by the strong dependence of electrochemical performance on externally applied stack pressure. Although high stack pressure can improve solid–solid interfacial contact and suppress degradation, it also imposes mechanical, manufacturing, and system-level constraints that are incompatible with practical cell and module designs. This review focuses specifically on the low-pressure operation of lithium-metal-based SSBs—defined here as operation under stack pressures of ≤2 MPa—by first examining the electrochemo-mechanical failure modes caused by insufficient mechanical confinement, including cathode-side contact loss and transport heterogeneity, anode-side void formation and current localization, and filament-mediated short-circuiting. Recent cathode, anode, anode-less, and cell-level pressure management strategies are then summarized to clarify how contact retention, transport robustness, Li deposition regulation, and pressure homogenization can reduce the need for high external compression. Finally, future research directions are suggested, including standardized low-pressure benchmarking, operando chemo-mechanical diagnostics, and scalable cell architectures, emphasizing that low-pressure operability should be regarded as a primary design criterion for practical SSBs.

abstract: Faced with the vast chemical space of materials, traditional trial-and-error approaches have become increasingly inadequate for rechargeable battery development because of long development cycles, high costs, and limited screening efficiency. Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly machine learning, has been applied to extract relationships among composition, structure, processing conditions, and material properties from computational and experimental data. These models support rapid property prediction, screening of large candidate spaces, and iterative selection of informative experiments. This review focuses on lithium-ion, sodium-ion, and zinc-ion batteries and provides an overview of the key technologies, application progress, challenges, and future directions of AI-driven rechargeable battery development. The technical foundations and general workflow are first outlined. Recent advances in AI applications to cathodes, anodes, liquid electrolytes, and solid-state electrolytes are then reviewed, with emphasis on high-throughput screening, performance prediction, and structure-property relationship mining. Current challenges are further analyzed in terms of data quality, descriptor construction, interpretability, and generalization capability. Future directions, including novel descriptor systems, AI-enhanced characterization, inverse design, and closed-loop development enabled by robotic automation and large language models, are also discussed in relation to intelligent battery research. This review is intended to provide a theoretical reference for the accelerated discovery of next-generation rechargeable battery chemistries and key materials.

abstract: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) have emerged as efficient electrocatalysts for the acidic oxygen reduction reaction (ORR). However, research on ordered HEAs remains limited, and the role of atomic mobility in catalytic performance is not fully understood. Here, a series of Pt 5 LaCeGdTb HEA nanoparticles with tunable atomic mobility were prepared via Joule thermal shock. We unravel the mechanism of the transformation from high to low atomic mobility in HEA nanoparticles at the single-particle level. The electrocatalytic performance is closely correlated with crystalline and electronic structures. Lowering atomic mobility significantly enhances electrocatalytic activity. The highly ordered Pt 5 LaCeGdTb (H-Pt 5 LaCeGdTb) exhibits a half-wave potential of 0.94 V in acidic ORR, a mass activity (MA) 13-fold higher than commercial Pt/C and a specific activity 8.3-fold higher. After 30k cycles of accelerated durability tests, the MA retention remains at 94.1%. Notably, the H-Pt 5 LaCeGdTb catalyst with low Pt loading exhibited superior Pt efficiency in proton exchange membrane fuel cells at elevated temperature compared to Pt/C. This order-dependent structure-performance relationship provides critical insights for the rational design of ordered HEAs catalysts.

abstract: Competitive adsorption between H 2 and CO x ( x = 1, 2) on oxide catalysts represents a primary limitation in hydrogenation reactions, where mutual site blocking suppresses activity and selectivity. This constraint hampers syngas conversion and CO 2 hydrogenation, yet strategies to decouple adsorbates remain elusive. Here, we show that competitive adsorption can be overcome through a partial-site-occupation mechanism that prevents surface saturation and enables independent activation. For a model ZnCr 2 O 4 @ZnO x system, in situ infrared spectroscopy directly reveals the simultaneous adsorption of H 2 with CO or CO 2 , in contrast to the mutually exclusive adsorption observed on pristine ZnO. Kinetic measurements link this decoupling to suppressed inhibition effects and altered reaction orders, driving improved catalytic performance. Density functional theory combined with temperature-programmed analyses further demonstrates that homolytic H 2 dissociation becomes thermodynamically self-limiting, resulting in intrinsically unsaturated surface coverages. These findings indicate competitive adsorption from an inherent constraint to a tunable surface property and establish practical design strategies for cooperative activation in ZnO-based oxide-catalyzed hydrogenation reactions.

abstract: Lithium bis(fluorosulfonyl)imide (LiFSI) is increasingly being utilized as a functional electrolyte additive in commercial lithium-ion batteries owing to its high thermal stability and favorable electrode compatibility. However, the concentration-dependent trade-off between the thermal safety and electrochemical performance of LiFSI-based electrolytes remains poorly understood due to the lack of a well-defined safe concentration boundary. Herein, a systematic investigation was conducted using LiFSI concentrations of 0–0.8 M, thermal abuse tests, and wide-temperature electrochemical evaluations (from −25 to 55 °C) within practical 52 Ah LiFePO 4 /graphite full cells. Thermal abuse tests established a critical LiFSI concentration threshold of 0.6 M, above which accelerated thermal degradation occurs. Exceeding this threshold triggered pronounced bis(fluorosulfonyl)imide anion decomposition, which reduced the thermal runaway trigger temperature ( T tr ) from 116.7 °C at 0 M to 52.0 °C at 0.8 M. Based on the observed thermal degradation mechanics, a safe-critical-hazardous (SCH) framework was established to identify the LiFSI concentration range that balances performance enhancement and abuse tolerance in commercial cells. Within this operational concentration window, the 0.4 M LiFSI formulation balances these competing metrics, delivering a power density of 394.5 W L −1 at −25 °C and 85.26% capacity retention after 1400 cycles at 45 °C, while maintaining T tr above 110 °C. These findings demonstrate that optimizing additive loading via the SCH framework transitions electrolyte development from empirical regulation to rational design. Consequently, it is suggested that future electrolyte configurations adopt concentration-guided strategies, such as multi-salt synergies or targeted interfacial passivation, to preserve high thermal stability ( T tr > 110 °C) without sacrificing wide-temperature operational efficiency.

Aluminum phosphate functionalization of graphite promoting interfacial lithium ion desolvation
abstract: Surface coating chemistry can promote Li + desolvation at graphite, provided that the coating does not hinder lithium intercalation. Here, we form a uniform aluminum phosphate (AlPO 4 ) layer approximately 10 nm thick on natural graphite by wet chemical deposition and annealing. The coating suppresses solvent co-intercalation and enables reversible graphite lithiation in strongly solvating propylene carbonate- and ether-based electrolytes; temperature-dependent impedance measurements indicate a lower apparent Li + desolvation barrier. After cycling, the AlPO 4 -containing layer remains on the graphite surface and supports the formation of a compact solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) with fewer organic decomposition products, as indicated by microscopy and secondary-ion analysis. In NCM523 full cells with a cathode areal capacity of approximately 2 mAh/cm 2 , the coated graphite reaches 80% state of charge in 7.4 min at 8 C and 30 °C, compared with 9.2 min for bare graphite. In separate tests at 0.1 C and −20 °C, the coated cells retain 62% of their capacity at 30 °C, compared with 26% for bare graphite. These findings establish phosphate coating chemistry as a means to couple faster interfacial ion transfer with more stable SEI formation.

title: Dynamic impedance characterization of lithium-ion batteries: Experimental insights and implications for battery management
abstract: Real-time impedance tracking holds significant potential in optimizing battery management, yet the understanding and practical utilization of dynamic impedance characteristics remain limited. In this research, a dynamic electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (DEIS) measurement protocol based on drifting-voltage suppression is developed to ensure reliable impedance extraction across various charge-discharge profiles. The DEIS measurements are performed on three cells, including a fresh NMC cell, an aged NMC cell, and a fresh LFP cell, at state of charge (SOC) levels of 80%, 50%, and 20%, and temperatures of 35, 25, and 15 °C. The results reveal two distinct dynamic impedance behaviors, which are quantitatively analyzed using the Mahalanobis distance and the coefficient of variation. Moreover, distribution-of-relaxation-time (DRT) analysis is employed to resolve relaxation features and provide qualitative insights into possible electrochemical contributions to the observed load-induced spectral distortions. Practical guidelines are provided for on-board DEIS implementation, real-time state monitoring, and dynamic impedance-based diagnosis.

abstract: Aqueous zinc-ion batteries (AZIBs) are promising candidates for renewable grid energy storage, but their development is limited by non-uniform zinc deposition, hydrogen evolution reactions (HERs), and byproduct growth at the zinc anode interface. Herein, a dual-regulation strategy integrating bulk solvation reorganization with interfacial dynamic electrostatic shielding is developed by introducing a trace amount of 1-butyl-3-methylimidazolium iodide (BMIMI, BI) into a Zn(OTf) 2 aqueous electrolyte. Multi-dimensional microscopic spectra and quantitative molecular dynamics simulations confirm that the co-incorporation of BMIM + cations and I − anions establishes a diversified I − -H 2 O-OTf − hetero-primary solvation sheath, disrupting the chemical degradation pathways caused by free water aggregation. Due to its electrostatic adsorption energy advantage on multiple crystal planes, BMIM + preferentially occupies active sites to form a dynamic cation shielding field. This forces Zn 2+ to diffuse away smoothly from local tip protrusions and induces lateral planar epitaxial growth along the dense (002) preferred crystal plane. Consequently, the electrolyte shows stability within the fundamental potential window during cyclic voltammetry tests, and the interfacial desolvation energy barrier decreases from 51.29 to 23.28 kJ mol −1 . This affords the Zn//Cu battery a stable Coulombic efficiency of 99.74%, and the Zn//Zn symmetric battery achieves a lifespan exceeding 7500 h under variable loads and high areal capacities. In full-cell applications, the cell maintains a capacity retention of 84.07% after 5000 cycles at a high current density of 2 A g −1 . Combined with ex-situ distribution of relaxation times and dynamic impedance evolution, this strategy confirms the feasibility of the system for industrial-grade variable-load energy storage scenarios.

A tale of two approaches for tuning optoelectronic properties in lead-based inorganic halide perovskite quantum dots
abstract: Inorganic perovskite quantum dots (IPQDs) are attractive emitters for optoelectronics because they combine variable photoluminescence (PL), high photoluminescence quantum yield (PLQY), narrow full width at half maximum (FWHM), and widely tunable bandgaps. Bandgap engineering is typically achieved through two complementary routes: (i) size-dependent quantum confinement, which becomes pronounced when the nanocrystal dimension approaches the exciton Bohr diameter, and (ii) compositional engineering by halide mixing and/or A-/B-site substitution. Yet these two tuning strategies are often discussed separately, and practical guidance on achieving a target bandgap while balancing carrier dynamics and stability remains limited. Here, we review and compare how confinement and composition tuning reshape the electronic structure and optoelectronic performance of lead-based IPQDs. Using representative CsPbBr 3 and CsPbI 3 systems, we summarize quantitative trends in emission energy (e.g., ∼450–520 nm for CsPbBr 3 via size control and ∼400–700 nm via composition tuning), exciton lifetimes (e.g., ∼540→170 ps at 4 K when the CsPbBr 3 QD size increases from 7 to 23 nm), linewidths, and phase/chemical stability. We further discuss synthetic controllability and scalability, and highlight key challenges and future opportunities for integrated approaches coupling confinement, composition, and surface chemistry.
